name: Hemp rust
summary: An institutional hemp rust differential characterized by orange-to-brown lesions on both leaf surfaces and erumpent orange spore masses from lower-surface pustules. These signs support a rust diagnosis, but a photograph does not establish Uredo kriegeriana, infection source, alternate host, or the full disease cycle.
affectedParts: whole plant and neighboring plants for distribution context
indicators: Compatible early lesions are light orange rather than white powder, purple-gray downy growth, black pycnidia, or a colorless puncture.
Lesions can darken from light orange to dark orange, brown, or rust-colored as they develop; color alone remains nonspecific.
The Tennessee guide describes poorly defined margins on early yellow-orange spots and possible merging of darkened lesions; an early spot need not have a sharply bounded ring.
The institutional composite pairs top and bottom views of one affected leaf with close views of an early upper-surface lesion and a lower-surface pustule.
The strongest visible sign is an orange powdery spore mass erupting from a pustule on the lower leaf surface.
The same-lesion upper/lower relationship is more informative than an isolated orange spot because rust structures may be concentrated on the underside.
Whole-plant and neighboring-plant views are still needed because the institutional composite does not establish canopy position, incidence, or field distribution.
A stable color reference and scale are needed to distinguish true orange sporulation from lighting, senescence, residue, frass, or dried spray deposits.
A rust-level label is strengthened by lesion-linked microscopy of compatible rust spores; species-level naming requires current taxonomic and laboratory support beyond this photograph.
exclusions: Purple-to-gray branching growth on the corresponding lower surface with an oomycete result supports downy mildew rather than rust.
White superficial colonies on either surface that wipe or reveal hyphae and conidia support powdery mildew.
Black embedded pycnidia and compatible conidia support Septoria; dark gray or black fuzzy growth supports a Bipolaris differential.
Mite, thrips, egg, webbing, frass, cast skin, or feeding evidence without lesion-linked rust spores supports arthropod injury or contamination.
Orange pollen, mineral residue, dried spray, soil splash, or foreign material that lifts from intact tissue excludes a symptom-only rust label.
A sharp lamp, spray, droplet, aisle, contact, or weather boundary with no pustules or compatible spores supports abiotic injury.
Uniform late-season yellowing or bronzing without erumpent pustules and with age-linked distribution supports senescence or nutrient/root-zone stress.
Representative microscopy or laboratory testing identifies another organism, or repeated active lesions lack compatible rust structures.

progression.description: Record cultivar, plant stage, canopy position, field or room map, recent weather and foliar inputs, plus matched apparently healthy leaves.
Tag attached leaves and capture full-leaf plus paired upper/lower views before visible powder is disturbed.
Reimage the same lesion as color becomes dark orange, brown, or rust-colored; do not infer a universal time interval from the institutional guide.
Capture an intact lower-surface pustule before and after gentle diagnostic sampling, with a scale and color reference, while preserving the matching upper-surface view.

Link microscopy, specimen identifiers, current taxonomic interpretation, and any molecular result back to the photographed plant and lesion; preserve query locus, accession, database access date, and voucher links when barcode matching is used.

lookAlikes: Pseudocercospora olive or sooty leaf spot
Dried foliar spray or mineral residue
confirmation: Capture the whole plant, canopy neighborhood, full leaf, and same-lesion upper- and lower-surface macro views with a scale, neutral color reference, and stable plant and lesion identifiers.
Revisit tagged lesions to document light-orange onset, darkening, and pustule eruption on the same tissue rather than assembling unrelated single frames.
Use magnification before sampling to distinguish an erumpent pustule and attached spores from residue, pollen, arthropods, frass, pycnidia, downy growth, or superficial mildew.

Collect intact representative pustules and lesion margins following a plant diagnostic laboratory protocol while retaining cultivar, age, site, weather, irrigation, leaf-wetness, and foliar-input metadata.

Require lesion-linked microscopy of compatible rust structures for a confirmed rust label and preserve measurements, images, preparer, method, and specimen identifiers. Photograph the intact pustule before scraping or slide preparation; link the mounting medium, preparation date, objective, lighting, and calibration to the same lesion. Record spore morphology and its originating structure together, and distinguish preparation-induced changes from in-plant progression.

Record unaided macro, dissecting-microscope pustule, and compound-microscope spore views as different capture types linked to the same lesion; visible orange powder does not show individual spore morphology or establish species.

Use current specialist taxonomic or validated molecular evidence when a Uredo kriegeriana species label matters; do not resolve the species from orange color, pustule appearance, host alone, or a guide image.

Ask the diagnostic laboratory to select a rust-appropriate locus: NPDN identifies 28S as the standard rust barcode and warns that ITS intragenomic variation limits separation. This general guidance does not validate a Cannabis-specific assay.

For Rust HUBB matching, retain the lesion-linked query sequence and locus, database access date, query coverage, identity, score and E value, reference accession and voucher, and host/country metadata. Dataset inference: require specialist interpretation instead of promoting a ranked best match directly to a species label.

For research histology, retain specimen linkage, preparation, probe, controls and imaging scale separately from intact-leaf images; a negative ISH image alone is not an exclusion result for hemp rust.

Keep sample collection, first observed lesion, photograph and laboratory confirmation dates separate. Dataset inference: retain site and exposure history as context, but do not assign infection date or transmission route from lesion color, regional reports or proximity to another hemp field.

Capture intact leaf surfaces before handling; wound-free leaves are not negative controls for rust. For cultivar comparisons, record the number of plants examined per cultivar, laboratory-linked rust status, plant age and exposure context; do not transfer leaf-spot trial ratings to rust resistance or infer resistance from unexposed symptom-negative plants.

Keep symptom-only, residue-uncleared, detached-leaf-only, unmatched-surface, specimen-unlinked, low-resolution, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, and rights-unclear samples out of confirmed labels and retain an unresolved classification when the evidence is incomplete.
immediateActions: Tag and photograph representative plants and intact pustules before handling or applying a product.
Limit movement of symptomatic propagation material and avoid disturbing powdery pustules until traceable samples are retained.
Map affected plants against cultivar blocks, airflow, field edges, recent weather, irrigation, foliar applications, and possible residue sources.
correctivePlan: Base management on a plant-linked laboratory result and current crop, site, and jurisdiction requirements rather than on orange color alone.
Contain confirmed diseased foliage and clean tools or handling surfaces as locally appropriate, then monitor tagged plants for new pustules.
Reassess the diagnosis if new lesions lack compatible lower-surface pustules or repeated representative microscopy does not support rust.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic foliage, debris, tools, or dislodged spores into clean areas.
Maintain traceable scouting across both leaf surfaces and neighboring plants so early lesions and new pustules can be separated from residue or senescence.
Manage avoidable prolonged foliage wetness and dense stagnant canopies where feasible without treating environmental response as retrospective confirmation.
warnings: Orange, brown, or rust-colored lesions are not by themselves diagnostic; the strongest visible rust evidence is an attached erumpent pustule with compatible spores.

The institutional guide supplies a visual differential but no plant-linked specimen ID, microscopy record, sequence result, cultivar, canopy distribution, incidence, or progression interval for the pictured leaves.

UF/IFAS states that the alternate host is unknown and that little is known about the disease cycle and epidemiology, so source, reservoir, timing, thresholds, prevalence, and yield effects must not be inferred.
The Uredo kriegeriana name is not visually resolvable and should remain provisional without current lesion-linked taxonomic evidence.

Rust HUBB is a changing, voucher-based reference resource, not a guarantee that the pictured hemp rust is represented or uniquely resolved; an ITS-only result or a top-ranked barcode match does not override unresolved specimen evidence.

The NPDN microscopy source is a general fungal-identification workflow, not a validated Cannabis rust assay, universal spore-size threshold, or proof of a particular Uredo species; qualified specimen-linked interpretation is still required.
Figure 9 is an attributed institutional three-panel reference under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; crops, panel extraction, derivatives, commercial reuse, and automated training are not permitted by this record.
The cross-host ISH study is not a validated hemp-rust assay or a field-color reference; unresolved staining or host transfer requires human review.
Unresolved symptom-only, residue-uncleared, detached, unmatched-surface, specimen-unlinked, low-resolution, and rights-unclear samples retain review flags.

sources.title: Field Guide to Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Diseases
sources.publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: The UF/IFAS guide describes hemp rust as orange, brown, or rust-colored lesions on both leaf surfaces, beginning light orange and darkening as disease progresses.
The guide identifies an erumpent orange spore mass from a lower-surface pustule as the strongest pictured rust sign, while still recommending plant-diagnostic-center confirmation.
UF/IFAS states that the alternate host is unknown and that little is known about hemp-rust epidemiology; wind dispersal is context, not proof of the source or timing of an individual infection.

UF/IFAS describes deposited rust spores that actively penetrate the leaf. Dataset inference: absence of visible wounds does not exclude rust, and a nearby injury does not establish the entry point of a photographed lesion; preserve intact-surface observations separately from handling damage.

UF/IFAS Figure 9 is an institutional three-panel hemp reference credited to Zachariah Hansen, University of Tennessee Extension; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 permits unchanged noncommercial display with attribution but not crops, derivatives, commercial reuse, or automated training.

sources.title: Hemp Disease and Pest Management
supportedClaims: The Tennessee W 916 guide describes poorly bounded yellow-orange spots, followed by darker orange-brown lesions that may merge; cultivar susceptibility differences remain unresolved.

The guide distinguishes lower-surface pustules visible without magnification, a pustule viewed with a dissecting microscope, and uredospores viewed with a compound microscope. Pustule visibility does not mean an ordinary photograph resolves individual spores or their species.

W 916 page 5 reports first confirmation at the UT Soil, Plant and Pest Center from East Tennessee samples collected on August 26, 2019, followed by observations across Tennessee and surrounding states; this is historical regional reporting, not a global first report or current prevalence estimate.

W 916 Table 2 lists nearby or possibly distant hemp fields as the most likely rust inoculum source and rain, wind, soil splash, workers, tools and equipment as likely dispersal routes; its footnote warns that disease understanding and these assignments may change with research.

W 916 Table 1 evaluates leaf-spot susceptibility in 2019 trials, while the rust section says cultivar susceptibility needs research. Dataset inference: leaf-spot ratings are not rust-resistance ratings; cultivar-associated rust observations need their own diagnosis, sampling denominators and exposure context.

sources.title: Rust HUBB - A new BLAST searchable online tool for identification of rust fungi
sources.publisher: National Plant Diagnostic Network, The Communicator, Volume 5, Issue 5
supportedClaims: NPDN describes ITS intragenomic variation as a limitation for separating rust fungi and identifies the 28S large ribosomal subunit as their standard barcode; this is order-level method context, not validation of a Cannabis rust species assay.

Rust HUBB uses barcodes from Arthur Fungarium vouchers and fresh collections, with updates as vouchered and verified sequences become available; preserve the database access date and voucher linkage rather than assuming fixed coverage.

Rust HUBB reports query coverage, score, E value, identity, voucher and collection numbers, GenBank accession, host and country metadata. Dataset inference: retain these with the lesion-linked query and specialist interpretation; a ranked best match alone is not a confirmed hemp-rust species label.

sources.title: Identifying Microfungi Under the Microscope - from Sample to Name
sources.publisher: National Plant Diagnostic Network, The Communicator, Volume 6, Issue 6
supportedClaims: The general diagnostic workflow starts with host and fungal-group assessment under dissecting microscopy or a 10–30× hand lens with oblique lighting, followed by low-objective compound-microscope scanning; these are different observation scales, not Cannabis-specific diagnostic thresholds.

The guide asks diagnosticians to record spore shape, size, septation, appendages, and the structure from which spores originate, then compare tentative identifications with current nomenclature and taxonomy. Orange powder alone does not supply that structural evidence.

Slide preparation can remove fungal tissue or dislodge structures by scraping into a mounting medium. Dataset inference: preserve intact-tissue images and preparation metadata separately from the resulting slide, rather than treating altered material as an untouched pustule or another in-plant progression stage.

sources.title: In situ hybridization for the detection of rust fungi in paraffin embedded plant tissue sections
sources.organization: Plant Methods (Ellison et al.; USDA-ARS collaborators)
supportedClaims: Ellison et al. tested rust-localizing ISH in chrysanthemum, gladiolus and soybean with uninfected controls, not Cannabis. This is cross-host method context, not validation for Uredo kriegeriana.

Soybean rust produced weak signal in one of five antisense-probe slides and needed further optimization; omitted digestion also eliminated signal in the chrysanthemum experiment. Dataset inference: a negative stain alone cannot exclude hemp rust.

The purple reaction product marked processed tissue-level hybridization signal; intracellular detail was not resolved. Dataset inference: stained sections are not natural leaf coloration or camera-visible intracellular infection.
